title: Locks on your accounts
hook: A 6-digit login code from your crypto app pops up on your phone. You didn't ask for it. A minute later a friend's account messages: "Oops, I sent my code to your number by mistake. Can you send it to me?"
card1: Apps that hold coins for you are protected by your password and a second step, called [[two-factor|two-factor authentication]] (2FA): a code from an app or a text message.
analogy1: 2FA is like a door with two locks. A thief who steals one key still can't get in, unless you hand over the second key yourself.
card2: A one-time code is that second key. Anyone who asks for it, even from a friend's account, is trying to get into your account. Never share codes.
card3: Use a long, different password for every account and keep them in a password manager. If one site leaks, the others stay safe.
adviceIntro: A video shares "security tips". Which ones are bad?

l1.text: Use the same strong password everywhere, so you remember it.
l1.why: If one site leaks, every account with that password is open.

l2.text: Turn on 2FA with an authenticator app.
l2.why: An app code is harder to steal than a text message.

l3.text: Send your login code to support if they ask.
l3.why: Support never needs your codes. Anyone asking is trying to log in as you.

l4.text: Keep long, different passwords in a password manager.
l4.why: It remembers them, so you never need to reuse one.

l5.text: Put your password in your bio so you don't forget it.
l5.why: Anything public can be seen by anyone.

code.prompt: Your friend's account writes: "I sent my login code to you by mistake, please send it to me!"

send.label: Send the code
send.before: You will send the 6 digits to this account.
send.what: The "friend" used the code to log in to your app account and sent away all your practice coins.
send.why: The code was yours: someone was logging in to your account and needed it.
send.how: Codes are sent to your phone exactly because only you should have them.
send.realLife: Never share a login code, whoever asks.

call.label: Call your friend to check
call.before: You will phone your friend before doing anything.
call.what: Your friend says they never sent anything: their account was hacked. You kept the code to yourself.
call.why: Checking another way was smart. But you never need to share a code, so you could just ignore it.
call.how: Scammers often use hacked accounts of people you know, because you trust them.
call.realLife: Tell your friend their account is hacked, and change your own password.

change.label: Don't share it, and change your password
change.before: You will ignore the request and change your password right away.
change.what: Someone had your password but couldn't get past the second lock. Now your password is new and they're locked out.
change.why: An unexpected code means someone typed your password and tried to log in.
change.how: 2FA stopped them. The new password takes away the key they already had.
change.realLife: An unexpected code is a warning: change your password right away.

q1.a: A second step, like a code, as well as your password
q1.b: Having two passwords for one account
q1.explanation: 2FA means something you know (your password) plus something you have (your phone or an app).

q2.prompt: You get a login code you didn't ask for. What does it mean?
q2.b: Someone may be trying to log in with your password
q2.explanation: Usually someone typed your password. Don't share the code, and change your password.

q3.prompt: Why use a different password for every account?
q3.a: If one site leaks, the others stay safe
q3.b: It doesn't matter as long as it's strong
q3.c: So you can change them every week
q3.explanation: A leaked password is tried on other sites right away. Different passwords stop that.

misc.twoPasswords: "2FA means two passwords." It's your password plus something you have, like your phone.
misc.onlyBanks: "Only banks use 2FA." Most apps offer it. Turn it on wherever you can.
misc.codeGlitch: "Random codes are glitches." Usually someone is trying to log in with your password.
misc.codeShare: "A friend needs my code." No one ever needs your code.
misc.reuseOk: "One strong password is enough everywhere." If it leaks once, every account that uses it is open.
misc.pwChange: "Changing passwords often is the point." Long, different passwords matter more than changing them often.

t1: Turn on [[two-factor|2FA]], ideally with an authenticator app.
t2: Never share a login code, whoever asks.
t3: Use long, different passwords and keep them in a password manager.
talk1: Which of our family's accounts have 2FA turned on?
talk2: What would we do if one of our accounts got hacked?
